utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic, aka Tuta, and Vinko Martinovic, aka Stela.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, did you take the solemn declaration made by the interpreter this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And who do you wish to be the next witness, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It will be me, Your Honour. Good morning. The next witness will be a member of the Spanish army. As with the prior Spanish army witness, the witness requested to have facial protection and a pseudonym, and there may be times when private session would be necessary concerning Rule 70 matters. The reasons are the same as those stated with the prior witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I wonder whether the legal counsel for the Spanish government will be present this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My understanding is yes, the same legal officer who was here on Tuesday, I guess it was, yes, will be here again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any objections from Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So I believe that the same conditions will apply to the presence of that legal counsel during the following proceedings. Would you please call the witness. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. While we are waiting for the witness, just a short question, because of some duties that I have tomorrow afternoon, I merely wanted to ask whether we shall be working tomorrow afternoon because I have to go on a short and urgent trip. Rather, we shall work tomorrow morning; I know that we are working every day. We do not have those breaks as in some other cases exist, and something has come up, and I have to do it tomorrow afternoon. So my question is: Shall we be working tomorrow afternoon or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Originally, we planned we will sit tomorrow afternoon because we have to make up the time we lost last week. Since you made this request to the Chamber, we will consider your request during the break. I hope I could give you a proper answer after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, on that point, I just have to say that we would be opposed to not sitting tomorrow. There is co-counsel here. One of the reasons for having co-counsel is so the case can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are only talking about tomorrow afternoon, not for the whole tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about also, tomorrow -- Friday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym for this witness will be LL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you very well indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please stand up and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I want to inform you that the Chamber has granted the protective measures, that your facial image will be protected in terms of any broadcast of these proceedings. So your face will not be shown. Also, your true name will not be used, and for that purpose, you will be referred to as "Witness LL." Please understand that no disrespect is intended by that, but it is simply for the purpose of protecting your identity. And in that regard, I will caution you to be mindful yourself of perhaps using your name or saying something that would be of such a nature that it might tend to identify you very specifically. I will also alert you that during some part of your testimony, it may be necessary that we go into what we call private session. The reason for that is -- what "private session" means is that the audio portion, that is, what you are saying or what is being said in the courtroom, will not be heard outside the courtroom, so that for some matters, they will be further protected in that way. Witness LL, is it correct that you are a professional soldier in the Spanish army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You currently hold the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, my apologies. I've skipped over the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness LL, I've omitted to show you this paper which makes the record of your true identity without saying your name in the courtroom. Again, for the reasons I've stated previously, don't state your name, but can you say yes or no: Is the name that is on that piece of paper indeed your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Witness LL, so you are a professional soldier currently holding the rank of major in the Spanish army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You joined the Spanish army academy in 1976 and left the academy in 1982 with the rank of lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were promoted to the rank of captain in 1986?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were promoted to the rank of major in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that while in the Spanish army, you have served on two peacekeeping missions to Bosnia-Herzegovina, first in 1993 and again in 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: This is correct. In the year 1993, with the Malaga group and with the Canarias unit. In 1997 with the Galicia Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention for purposes of today's testimony to your time there in 1993, is it correct that you were - as you just mentioned - you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of the Spanish army peacekeeping force from January 1993 to approximately the 15th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as you mentioned a moment ago, for the first part of this tour, it was with the Malaga Task Force, and for the second part the Canarias group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Witness LL, I understand that during this first tour, you were the captain in charge of a unit called the Deep Reconnaissance Patrol.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. This is "Patrulla de Reconcimiento en Profundidad" in Spanish, Depth Reconnaissance Patrol that belonged to the group of our Special Operations Unit of the legion, BOEL.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you briefly describe to the Chamber the function or mission of the Deep Reconnaissance Patrol.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, the mission of the Deep Reconnaissance Patrol in the area of responsibility they had in Bosnia-Herzegovina was to provide security to Spanish troops in the area under their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, we have heard from other military witnesses sometimes the terminology such as G-2 or S-2, such terminology is used. Did any such terminology apply to you in your unit, and if so, can you describe that to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: G-2, S-2 is the person in charge in the higher-ranking officers, everything that has to do with information and security. And my unit worked for this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For S-2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. The second section at the level of the G-2. G-2 is their highest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is it correct that you arrived in Split, Croatia, on approximately the 12th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I was near Split with a unit in a place in Divulje that had been assigned to Spanish troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were you able, in fact, before you left, before you departed Spain, to assemble a group of approximately 30 soldiers to comprise this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. Personally, I chose all the members of my patrol for this very specific mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you stayed in this village or location near Split for approximately one week; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you and your unit then transfer to a new base of operations or headquarters at Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber a bit more about how your unit was organised? Did you have sub-units in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: My unit I set up on the basis of carrying out patrols. Each patrol had six -- five or six men, and each patrol was under the command of a sub-officer, an officer or noncommissioned officer, and they covered the whole area of responsibility under Spain's responsibility. Apart from this, we wanted to have permanent contact with these patrols. Therefore, I set up two radio stations with HF system, high-frequency system, in order to be sure that there would be permanent communication between myself and my patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as to yourself, Witness LL, did you both operate in the field yourself and also work at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning, I wanted to see how the real situation stood. I wanted to understand the problems in this country, the special circumstances involved. Therefore, I spent much more time in the field. I wanted to have personal contact with the people living there, rather than keep to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in your organisation, in your unit -- or the larger unit, that is, not your individual unit, but in the Spanish army contingent, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: My superior officer in the Malaga Task Force was the head of Malaga Task Force, Commander Fontella. And then in the operations area, he became lieutenant-colonel. Now, later, with the Canarias Tactical Group, I was under Major Acuna, who was head of the second section of the Canarias group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to go to -- to direct your attention to March of 1993. At that time, did you establish a detachment of your unit in Mostar itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. The head of HQ, Major Fontella, asked me to leave Jablanica and go to Mostar in order to set up contacts with the factions, the two factions, HVO and Armija. Therefore, I took with me several patrols, set them up in Mostar. But I was ordered by Commander Fontella to go to Medjugorje. And with this, it was much easier for me to set up contacts, both in Mostar and in the surroundings of Mostar, Citluk, Ljubski, Slavina, Kresevo, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, around this time or before that, had the overall Spanish army contingent located its principal base at Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, your unit produced certain reports called INTREPs, I-N-T-R-E-P, and INTSUMs, I-N-T-S-U-M. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. Information was used to draft the INTREPs, the INTSUMs, and the SITREPs, which were reports on situation, so for the third section of the HQ that dealt with operations. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what the difference is between an INTREP and an INTSUM?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: An INTREP is a summary of information which refers to one specific day. An INTSUM is a summary of information that has to do with a longer period of time, let's say, 10 to 15 days. The INTSUM, therefore, gathers all the data, all the information from all the daily INTREPs, and the INTSUM refers to all these INTREPs. We could say that it's a sort of summary of several INTREPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do these INTREPs and INTSUMs sometimes not simply report information but also provide or involve some analysis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The INTREPs or the INTSUMs usually have a small commentary made by the person who is drafting the report, sort of an analysis of all the information that has been included in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your unit, the Deep Reconnaissance Patrol, who performed the analysis in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: I was the person who had the responsibility of drafting the INTREPs and doing the analysis, but then these later could be completed by the commander in chief or by the second section of the HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And these reports that your unit made, they would be sent to who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: All these reports would leave the Malaga Task Force or the Canarias Task Force and be sent to the multinational division southeast, and to the rapid action section of the Spanish army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During your first tour in Bosnia in 1993, what was your overall assessment of the reliability of the information that you were able to obtain and on which these reports were based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, as far as these reports are concerned, I drafted them basically with regard to contacts I had with military staff, but from both groups, HVO and Armija; also contacts with civilians living in towns and -- and the degree of reliability had to do with the fact that somebody was giving me the information, this friend that was giving me information, wanted to tell the truth to me or not. And then we could later carry out a contrast to see whether, in real fact, there was this attack or whether people were transferred from one town or another, whether this really happened as the information I had received beforehand said it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness LL, is it accurate to say that as your tour, your first tour, extended into approximately the April period, did you see the situation in the Spanish army's area of responsibility becoming more difficult with the tensions between the Croats and the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Tension developed, escalated. Insecurity developed as well. Problems increased progressively, and I realised that this was happening when the Malaga group was relieved by the Canarias.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the Canarias group came in approximately when, early to mid-April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I am unable to tell you the exact date, the exact day in April. I think that the date is in the documents. However, I do believe it was in April when the one group relieved the other. And Colonel Zorzo and Colonel Morales were the two officers involved in this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, during this time and thereafter, through the remainder of your first tour, did the Spanish army have complete freedom of movement in the area, in its area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: No. This freedom of action, freedom of movement always depended on the -- well, on the readiness of various patrols of the factions on the ground, either at the checkpoints or under the orders that were given them. And then our freedom depended on that, whether we could carry out -- whether we could move or carry out our actions. However - sorry - once -- once we obtained the authority to enter a town and patrol a town, we could not again move freely, because that was not our own country. So we had, of course, to act under certain limitations regarding the population, regarding the military, and above all, not to interfere or not to upset either of the two factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you familiar, sir, with what's called an OrBat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain to the Chamber what an OrBat is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: OrBat is an organigramme. It is a graph showing the composition of units in an army, and it can be extended with names of the commanders, the composition of the units, the armaments, their materiel, their areas of responsibility, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the term itself, "OrBat," is that essentially an abbreviation for "Order of Battle"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber whether during the time of the transition from the Malaga force to the Canarias group, did you perceive that either of the warring sides, any of the warring sides, took advantage, if you will, of this transition period in terms of perhaps the International Community understanding its organisation and structure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: I think that yes, the transition period at the time when one unit was relieved by another in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a very critical moment for us since one unit has to brief very well and explain everything to the relieving unit. That time overlapped in time with a moment of tension, with a major movement of people and vehicles on the roads, and I can tell you that we passed some very difficult moments. It took us quite some time to be able to establish the state of the units and to find out about their intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you assist the Chamber with whether those difficulties were more pronounced with one of the warring parties than the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: I wanted to establish the same contacts with all these units, but it turned up that there was much more movement on the part of the HVO, much more change on the part of the HVO than in the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention to a time. Were you introduced at some point to a man named Ivan Andabak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity to meet personally that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you just tell us in a few -- in a moment or two the circumstances in which you met Mr. Andabak and where you were when that happened and what was taking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: That individual was -- that person was introduced to me by the Colonel Zorzo, who was the commander of the Malaga Tactical Group. That person was the colonel of the special forces of the HVO at the time. And since I also came from the special forces, we communicated very easily, and that also means that there was a mutual confidence, that we trusted one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know how it was that Colonel Zorzo had come to know Mr. Andabak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, please, is it correct that Mr. Andabak was married to a Spanish woman and in fact had himself lived in Spain for a time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. After the close communication with this person whom I respected, whom I held in high respect, and others, he told me that he was in Spain in Tito's time and that he was married to a Spanish lady called Juani. I had the opportunity to meet both her and her daughter or their daughter at a dinner to which I was invited in the house where Colonel Andabak and his family lived at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you there for a moment. Before we continue about the dinner, did Andabak also speak fluent Spanish?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. And this allowed me to establish a much higher level of confidence to discuss personal topics in a military environment, to talk about family matters, to talk about children, to talk about the conflict. And in this way, I could manage to incorporate myself, to integrate myself in the problems that existed in the country, the intentions of the two sides, and to thus try to help and to try to achieve, to obtain a clear picture of the general situation in order to see whether one of the intentions or some of the -- there could be some plans or some attempts against the Spanish forces, something that could threaten their security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During your tour in Bosnia in 1993, did you meet anyone else with the HVO that spoke fluent Spanish?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: At present, I don't remember meeting any other HVO members with a knowledge of Spanish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That enabled you, sir, to have particular contact with Mr. Andabak; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. We talked quite a lot, and we met frequently, whether by accident or because we had set these meetings. This was very pleasant for both of us. If he or I went to Mostar, and then we'd stop and talk. It was very pleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness LL, I hope I'm not stepping on something that you would consider to be sensitive, but I would think as a general matter, it was no secret that part of what you were trying to do was obtain information from various people that you met during your tour in Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. One of my tasks was indeed to obtain whatever information possible about the intentions of both sides at the time, because we were not -- we were not there to be served but to serve the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to help them to bring about peace and ensure humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But whatever relationship you indeed had with Mr. Andabak, I take it, sir, what you're telling the Chamber is this was not an entirely social relationship.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Absolutely. All the social activities that would be initiated by me would be driven by this chief motive, to obtain information. Socialisation, social contacts were a way of -- in which we could gain confidence and, thus, obtain information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we come back to this dinner, which I believe you've told us was at Mr. Andabak's house, can you just tell the Chamber, during your tour in 1993, approximately how many times in total were you at Mr. Andabak's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, I don't really quite remember it right now, but I was -- I received such invitations to his residence, to his house, on some five or six different occasions, from the first day I met him until the final day in July when I went to say goodbye; not only to him but primarily to his wife and his family. They were Spaniards, and I wanted to say how happy I was to have met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back to this dinner, did you meet some other Bosnian Croat at this dinner at Andabak's house, the first one that you mentioned a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, I met the whole family of Ivan Andabak. I met his deputy, and I also met his friend, a friend who was very important to him, and that was Tuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who introduced you to Tuta at that dinner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: The formal introductions were made by Mr. Ivan Andabak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, please, how it was, if you remember, what words did Mr. Andabak use in introducing Tuta to you and saying who he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, after all these years, I cannot really repeat the words. But what he said, that this was a very influential person both in the world of politics and in the world of economy of business and in military life, and that it was his commander, that he worked with him and that he was first and foremost his friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just now you said, "And that he was his commander." Please explain between these two individuals, Andabak and Tuta, who was whose commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: During the conversation at that time, I understood that Tuta issued orders to Ivan Andabak, that he was the commander, that Ivan Andabak was the chief of his special forces. But above him, there was Tuta, who planned operations or, perhaps, made a recommendation regarding the instructions, regarding the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to know the base of operation, so to speak, for Tuta and Andabak during 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I came to know both the building which housed Ivan Andabak's office, his headquarters, and another building which -- where he was -- where he often spent time, too, a different building from the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me go back to what you observed about the relationship between Andabak and Tuta during that evening or any other time. When you saw the two of them interact with one another, can you tell the Chamber, was one of them more deferential to the other, treat the other as, again, one's superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, at the time, regarding this kind of relationship, you know, you were at a dinner, which is very agreeable, and you don't notice much the hierarchy. What I could see was the friendship which existed between Andabak and Tuta. As for the deference, I could see that he was very happy, that he was very happy, very glad to be with Tuta, to be his friend; I could see that. Tuta was very smart, very dignified, highly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ranking socially, and quite evidently above Ivan Andabak's level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, during or after dinner that evening, did you have a conversation, ongoing conversation, with Andabak and Tuta for several hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. It was a rather long dinner, and there was a lot -- there were long conversations there, and there we had the opportunity to learn about Ivan Andabak's life and Tuta's, because that time, everybody was relaxed, there was mutual trust. And there we learned the histories of both those persons, why they were in their situation, what were their intentions, and why precisely they were in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple questions following on that. Did Tuta himself tell you some of his personal history? Did he tell you in his own words about himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. He, in a way, supplied me with a summary of the story of his life, why he was in that particular situation at the time. He created the impression of a man who had left all the commitments he had outside his country to come and help his country. He wanted to invest all his effort, all that he had to defend the cause of his country and of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also said a moment ago that -- you also said that they described their situation and what their intentions were. What did Andabak and Tuta say about their intentions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, the future was clear at the time to them. They were fighting for a country where Bosnian Croats would predominate, and their intention was to set up the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, expelling the Muslim people from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is that what Tuta and Andabak said, it was their intention, their purpose, to expel all the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was anything said about the role of Mostar in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. To them, Mostar could serve as the capital of the -- of that republic, a very important one. It was, for them, the key city with the largest number of population. And they disliked in a way -- but they disliked the presence of Muslims in the area. And because of that, they wanted to try to take precedence and to get rid of the Muslim population in the area, to apply pressure to get rid of the Muslims in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now we're moving on beyond this dinner. Mr. Andabak continued, is it correct, as one of your most regular HVO contacts during your tour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who else --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Sorry. But he was not the only one. I had many other contacts with HVO militaries, because I did not want to focus on him alone. However, he became, for me, one of the pivotal men because it was easy for me to communicate with him in Spanish and because he had come to trust me, perhaps much more than other men, than other military either in the HVO or in the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to come back to some of your other contacts in a moment, but I probably omitted one thing that I should have asked you about the dinner at Andabak's house. Was there an interpreter present at this dinner, either provided, if you will, by the Croat side, or one arranged by the Spanish army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Zorzo had his interpreter with him, I mean the one who always travelled with him, and he was the only one who used that interpreter. But since at the dinner Mr. Tuta spoke Italian, we could, up to a point, converse directly without the need to resort to an interpreter's help.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back to your contacts, apart from Mr. Andabak, you said there were some others. Can you name one or two of your other principal HVO contacts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. But I think that this is a professional secret, and I, therefore, cannot tell you which were the sources of information that I had. What I was trying was to see to it that all that Ivan Andabak told me could be also confirmed by -- corroborated by other people, that is, I didn't rely solely on him. And on some occasions, of course, there was no other source because it was much easier for me to see Ivan Andabak than to get into the headquarters and try to talk to a specific person. But, as I must repeat, there were other sources, there were other friends, both in the -- in their main staff and outside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: The only one I can mention, because I do not think it is particularly important, there was the head of a brigade which was quartered in Ljubuski who also became a friend. He and -- his name was Tomic, and I met him several times. I visited him at his home on a number of occasions, and we also met in a coffee bar in the area of Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, during your tour, sir, did you become familiar with such HVO officers -- and I say "familiar." I'm not suggesting necessarily in a personal way, but in the course of your duties, did you become acquainted with the names Petkovic, Bozic, and Lasic, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I met those persons and military personnel too, since the contacts with Colonel Zorzo happened on a regular basis. And in almost all cases or most of them, Colonel Zorzo took me along to these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you consider those, for instance, Petkovic and Bozic, to be the same sort of information contacts as, say, Ivan Andabak was, or were they at some different level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Naturally, the level of relationship with them was completely different. They were the top brass. They could inform us openly, and all the information from them could be done in an open and clear form. They could tell us about the general situation and also about the intentions. They could speak about that to Colonel Zorzo. But as with Tomic and as with Andabak, he [as interpreted] pursued perhaps more details, more specific details about the units, the kind of training, the armament they had, the armament they used. And all these questions, when put to gentlemen at a higher level, are less important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, just for clarification, you said just now -- at least it came across it the transcript -- it says, "He pursued perhaps more details," et cetera. Who is the "he" that you're referring to there? Or perhaps I don't know if it was translation. Were you referring to yourself, persons that you pursued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: I personally wanted to get to details. But just as well, they, logically, because there was this flow of personal information, and it didn't cost me anything to tell them about our intentions, because this was open information, very sincere. And I also told them about our intentions, about our assistance. This was something that was a regular -- a regular matter. I mean, it happened all the time between them and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go forward, please. You mentioned a few minutes ago that you were aware of -- that Andabak had one or two offices or places where he worked in the city of Mostar. Was one of those in the main headquarters of the HVO General Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was on the ground floor. One would enter there and then be able to -- to greet him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know -- do you recall anything about the approximate location of this second building where Mr. Andabak had an office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, I know that that building was not next to the previous building. There was a street which had been blocked by the police or the military of the HVO, and one could -- the situation on the map or the references I have, I don't think I could be able to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Let me direct your attention to the 7th of May, 1993. Did you see Ivan Andabak on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, the 7th of May exactly, I would have to look at my papers and see whether I could find some notes with this date on it. I saw Ivan Andabak a day or two before the violence escalated in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Mr. President, Your Honours, I notice that this witness is reading from some statement, and I would appreciate it greatly if this witness could tell us what statement he has in front of him that he is reading from in order to answer the questions put forth to him by Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that is a legitimate request.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a statement I made, and I think that everybody has it. I made this statement before, before I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's correct that after this witness arrived in The Hague, he was given the opportunity to review his prior statement, as most witnesses are. I must say I did not -- I was not aware that he had it with him. So I will defer to the Chamber's wishes and to have -- if you want to have that withdrawn or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, my problem with this obviously stems from the fact that if the witness cannot remember anything on his own recollection but must refer to a written statement previously made, then we must just put that statement into the record. I cannot cross-examine that statement. It denies my client the right to confront the witnesses against him, if in fact that is the case. If he is just having the statement sitting there in front of him, that would be a different situation. I am unclear at this point if the witness is using that statement for every answer or if he is just using it to refresh his recollection for some questions. Do you understand my position, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we have to say that not everybody in this Trial Chamber has got the previous statement made by the witness. Secondly, the live testimony is to hear what the witness is going to tell us on the spot, rather than refer to any previous statement. And before the witness uses any supporting materials, this Chamber should be properly informed about the origin, the source of that material. So, Mr. Scott, could you advise your witness to withdraw that statement in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness LL, I'm going to ask you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the easiest thing is just the usher can just collect that at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness LL, I'll come back to you in just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to make a further record about this, because in my observing the witness since he commenced testifying, he has not -- he has not in fact been making frequent reference to anything in front of him, which is one of the reasons I didn't notice that he had anything there. So I don't want the record to suggest or any comments by counsel to suggest that the witness has been sitting there frequently leafing through a document. I don't think the record would show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think we've noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness LL, let me address you on this, please, so there's no confusion. If on some particular point, you believe your memory is exhausted and it would refresh your memory to review a document, you can indicate that? But of course, as you've heard the president say, what the Chamber is primarily interested in, of course, is your live testimony to the best of your memory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I was asking you about seeing this Mr. Andabak. And perhaps you didn't remember the particular day, but let me give you another point of reference in time, if it will assist you, and maybe you can use that point of reference. Are you familiar with the fact, sir, that on the 9th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. President, I take it it can be hardly disputed at this point in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But on the 9th of May, there was a large military action in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. On the 9th of May, there was a military event which was, in fact, the attack that occurred between HVO and BH forces in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm not going to go to that just this moment. But with that date in mind, can you tell the Chamber, did you see Mr. Andabak in Mostar a short time before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that I saw him one evening in his second HQ. I saw Mr. Ivan Andabak, and he was wearing campaign uniform. It was a black uniform. He was wearing grenades. He had arms. He had munition. And I asked him in a direct fashion, "what are you preparing?" And he said that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he was preparing, he was preparing himself to go and attack, to carry out military action, and that heads would roll that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After hearing this from Mr. Andabak, did you have contact with any other representatives of either side -- or I should, perhaps, with three sides, say any side of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I said that above all, what we wanted is to have maximum transparency and neutrality in any activity we carried out. So I went to the HQ of BH. I went to the HQ of his brigade, which was also in Mostar, and I spoke with the chief, General Midhat Hudruk, and I saw that they also were preparing themselves. And I asked them, "What's going on?" Because I was a bit alarmed, because the attitude had changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry to stand up like this, Your Honour, Mr. President, but page 25, line 2 the witness just indicated that he spoke to the chief, General, and it's not on the screen. Could we please have that spelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We also noticed that. But Mr. Meek, let us hear the witness first, because you are not objecting to the question asked by the Prosecutor; just to make one specific point clear. Yes, Mr. Scott. Will you please make it clear for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going to come back to that very point myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you can, sir, and maybe -- I'm not sure if you -- well, can you tell us, if you can, the spelling of the name of the person you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: I am not an expert in names, and I'm not an expert in this language. However, I do believe that in a report, the name could be Midhat, M-i-j-a-d [as interpreted], Guodouk, G-u-o-d-o-u-k [as interpreted]. The first letter is an "H."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Approximately, because I'm not an expert in languages and in spelling. And I'm very sorry that I offended the lawyer because I did not put forward this detail correctly. But it's very difficult for me to give you more details on the way in which the name and the last name of this person is spelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness LL, I'm sorry, I thought -- frankly, I thought you spelled it rather well, but I'm still not sure it came through on the transcript particularly well. It sounded to me it was something like H-u-d-r-u-k.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said when you went to the ABiH headquarters, you saw that they were also preparing, and you asked them about that. And if you recall anything more, what did you learn from them at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. Now, General Midhat Hudruk and Humo told me that they knew about what was going to happen, and they were expecting an attack from BHO [as interpreted]. I was alarmed. I was very concerned about this instantaneous change in the situation. Therefore, I went to my HQ in Medjugorje; and there, I made a due note of the situation in order to inform Colonel Morales directly, and this is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment because, again, we probably need to have some details more clear. Just now, in addition to Hudruk, you mentioned a second name, which I believe it was something like Humo. Was it H-u-m-o?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's Humo. It's written just like that, the transcript on the screen. I've never seen his name in written form. I only have heard it being spoken, and I don't know whether this is the right way to spell this name, but I think it's approximately right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was he another Armija officer at the ABiH headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, he was the second in command of the brigade that was under Hudruk. He was a young man. And according to what he told me, he was an architect, or at least he had studied architecture, and he was always preparing himself with the whole of his HQ to receive an attack. And this is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Two other points here just before we move forward. It may be important to tell us, when you say the ABiH headquarters, of what particular unit? Was this the overall headquarters, or are you talking about a particular brigade or component?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, at that time, according to what I was told by the members of this HQ, it was the 41st Brigade of this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then finally, I apologise for slowing you down on your testimony. But back now some lines, you said that they were expecting --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm looking, Mr. President, back up at approximately line 10 on page 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said they were expecting an attack from the BHO. I think maybe some certain letters have been confused there. Who were they expecting? Who were the ABiH officers expecting an attack from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. Armija was expecting an attack from HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you told us, then, you went on to say that when you then received this information from both sides, including Mr. Andabak, you went to Colonel Morales at Medjugorje and advised him of these developments. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. And from that time on, he ordered, Colonel Morales, that is, to have alert situation in all the Spanish units and to set up a military convoy with armour and vehicles in order to patrol the city of Mostar and reinforce our presence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you and Colonel Morales go with this convoy or patrol, including armored vehicles, into Mostar to patrol the city, either that day or the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. That same day, we started before 12.00 midnight of the 7th, and we ended the operation on the 8th, early morning, about 2.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you do? Just briefly tell the Chamber, what did you do in conducting this exercise in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, what we did was to be there, to have a presence there, different forces of Spanish forces under UNPROFOR in the city of Mostar in order to try to intimidate; in other words, to secure protection of the city proper and to try to discover information or ideas that could lead to us thinking that there would be an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, when the major components of this convoy or the series of patrols left Mostar. You said early that morning, did you -- and I'm not going to mention any names here. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think, Mr. President, it's critical to this aspect of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But did you leave a small unit of men on an observation point on a hill overlooking Mostar that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. That day, in the afternoon, we left a group of us, a patrol of us on a hill in order to see any action that could occur in the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I want to move forward, then, to the 9th of May. Can you tell us what happened that morning. What came to your attention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, what happened is that we had communication with this patrol with a radio, and they told us that attacks were occurring in the city of Mostar and they came from the HVO towards the Muslim area and that these attacks were shelling, bombs falling in a Muslim area, and also there were shooting with anti-aircraft guns against buildings, against the HQ of the 41st Brigade of the BH army. And also a concentration of people, of staff, in the football stadium in Mostar that were protected by policemen within the football stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- on that last point, you said there was a concentration of people, and you said "staff." I'm not sure -- what do you mean by "staff"? "Staff" in the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. What I mean is that -- well, this is something we were able to assess later. At the beginning, we saw a lot of people in this football stadium, many people on the grass. And then lately -- later, we realised there were older people, there were women, there were children, and they were led towards this football stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you notice a number of buses near the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. Outside the stadium, there were many, many buses, civilian buses. Twenty, thirty civilian buses. And these people were transferred, people who had been concentrated in the football stadium. There were policemen or armed forces around them, and they were taken on a road towards the area where we were. Therefore, it was easier for us to identify the type of people that were being transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, before we come back to that, you may have gotten -- I may have gotten us a bit ahead of ourselves. When you got this information, when you received this radio report from the observation point left around Mostar, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to ask that that last answer be redacted. I was just about to caution the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness LL, on some of these names, I'm going to caution you not to use them. I have not -- I have not cautioned you about some of the senior officers because I would take it it was more or less publicly known, the presence of some of the senior officers in the country at that time. But as to some of these other individuals, unless there's particular -- unless you think it's particularly necessary, it may be better just not to use their names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So you took -- you assembled this group after reporting to Colonel Morales, and you yourself went to this overlook point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. I took contact myself with a group I had on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you'd already begun to tell us some of the things you could observe, and let me just come back to it in this way if I can: Were you able to see yourself these -- what you were telling us about a few minutes ago? This is not only what you were being told on the radio, but were you able to see these things you've told us about a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I was very impressed to see that the people that were guarding these people were treating them as if these people were prisoners. And also, I was impressed by direct shooting with machine-guns towards the HQ of the 41st Brigade of the BH army, including the concentration of direct fire. And this brought about fire inside the HQ, inside the building proper. And sometimes they were shooting with tracing bullets, which help the shooting itself. It's easier to shoot with these bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the clock. If you would like us to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, before you continue, I will ask Madam Registrar to take the solemn declaration from that interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to address the Chamber for a moment. I was looking back at the transcript in, I hope, an extreme abundance of caution. But in terms of the question that was raised about the witness having a copy of his statement on the witness stand, for counsel and the Chamber, I am looking at the transcript page 23, starting about line 13. As part of my comments, I said, "So I don't want the record to suggest or any comments by counsel to suggest that the witness has been sitting there frequently leafing through a document. I don't think the record would show that." And Her Honour Judge Clark commented, "I think we've noticed that." To be perfectly honest, I took Judge Clark's comment to be an affirmation or agreement with what I was saying. But if I misinterpreted it, I wanted to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think I meant to indicate -- I thought that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. transcript didn't really reflect that, that I meant to indicate that we have noted that this witness was not consulting his notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark. I appreciate that very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe all those transcripts will be checked during the night, so there's no problem for you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness LL, to continue on, at one point before the break, you said that these buses that you could see leaving the football stadium in Mostar were coming toward the direction or toward the location where you were observing these events. And can you tell us, did some of these buses, in fact, pass quite close to you and your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you just tell the Chamber a bit more about what you saw in terms of could you see the people on the buses and what kind of people were on these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. It passed right in front of me, because I had the opportunity to stop the convoy which was moving and was being conducted by the HVO and so that I could see that inside the buses. There were very many people, civilians, women, small children, and elderly. The faces were very expressive, so that I asked the military where were they taking them. And they told me that I could not be there and that I should leave immediately. And during this conversation, through a window, a civilian threw at me a small piece of paper through the bus window, which was open, asking me for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say that you engaged in a conversation with someone associated with this convoy, and then this same person then indicated that your presence was not wanted there, who are you talking about? Could you identify -- not by name, but what kind of person was this and with which armed force was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. The convoy was being escorted and led by a car, a car -- a military car belonging to the HVO army. So I spoke to an HVO member. And all the escorts, all the guards there were also from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as these -- as the buses then went by, you said this piece of paper was thrown out the window to you. Let me just ask you, did you feel at that moment you were in a position to intervene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: My intervention, no, it could not be done because I had to have a special authorisation for any intervention. My intervention was to try and dissuade them. But I could do it only orally, I could intercede only orally with the military who were taking the convoy to ask them, therefore, to let those people go. But they were behaving increasingly violently. And to avoid an armed conflict, that is, to avoid any fire being opened, I had to withdraw from the area and to let them go on with what they were doing. However, we continued to tape the movement of the buses, which were heading for the Heliodrom -- for the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was what I was going to ask you next. From this vantage point -- or if you moved about, you can tell the Chamber that, please. But from the places where you were conducting these observations, could you see these buses go so far as a place called the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We were on a dominant position, because the airport is in a valley. So that from where we were, we could see very clearly the final destination of all those people who were in those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned just now -- it may have come up in your prior testimony. I'm not sure if you mentioned it so much, but you were filming. Did this group -- the group that you were with, at that time you had a video camera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel -- the chief of the Malaga Tactical Group had authorised me to take a video camera along so as to film all that was happening. So I went on filming this whole sequence so that I could have one proof more which I would take to the head of the Canarias Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on that point, Witness LL, just to probably answer the question on everyone's mind in the courtroom, have you tried to find this videotape in the records of the Spanish army, and is it correct that at this point in time, that it has not been able to locate -- it's not been possible to locate that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I tried, as far as I could, to find out the lot of this tape, and I haven't managed to find it to this day. However, I hope that I will be able to find it eventually and to offer it to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I realise, sir, it's not your individual ability to make this commitment, of course. It has to come from your government. But are you willing to continue to make efforts to locate that tape and, if so, provide it to this Chamber before the trial's -- if it's found before the trial is concluded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is a historical fact, that is, the reality which is reflected in this recording. This is a part of the -- of history which I lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it will be of interest for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let's continue with your observations on this -- the day of the 9th of May. As you were moving about that day, but come to Citluk, and did you happen to make any observations around that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. When I left the area where the buses were and we were filming, I quickly headed towards Medjugorje. And before I arrived there, towards the area of Citluk, we heard the sound of guns firing. From the road we could not see it properly, but we could hear that, however. And I therefore took another road in order to see -- in order to try to establish what was the origin of this fire, and could I see that there were two field guns. I cannot give you the exact calibre of those guns, but they could be of more than 100 millimetres, with long barrels, that is, long range. And at that moment, an HVO officer turned up, was there, who was ordering to fire one of these guns, and they were targeting Mostar. They were pointing at Mostar. Now, logically, I could not see from the position that I was at where these projectiles fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you about that in this -- to this extent: I know you perhaps didn't have a chance to inspect the guns in great detail, but from what you could see, were these the type of weapons, based on your military knowledge, which would have the range to reach Mostar from that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Absolutely. Their range could be between 15 and 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This HVO officer that you encountered, did he then come to essentially ask you to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. He did not like our arrival and our presence. He was a lieutenant. And I think perhaps to win our confidence, he invited us to fire ourselves. I flatly refused to do that, and I told him that he had to go, to leave, and that he was not allowed to open such fire against the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: But -- and I refused to leave until they stopped firing, saying that I couldn't allow any such action. And then to intimidate us, he turned the guns and turned them on to the vehicles with which we had arrived there. As I could not imagine what those people intended to do, I decided to peacefully leave the place without intimidating them and to go and report immediately to my superior, the commander of the Canarias Tactical Group. Before that, while I was talking with this lieutenant, we made some photographs which I could not find. I could not find these photographs afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Two questions about that. In fact, sir, do you recall that during this -- around this occasion - excuse me - around this time that some film was confiscated from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Correct. The lieutenant saw that we were making some photographs from the car, and he got very angry and told me to hand him over the camera and the film. And I told him that it was a personal camera. And to calm him down, we took out an ordinary camera from the car with a film that had not been used here, and I gave it to him so that he would keep quiet. The camera with which we were making the photographs we kept so that I could give the cartridge -- rather, the film, I could give this roll to the chief of the Canarias Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before moving forward with your testimony, one further question: It might be a small point, but when you say that these artillery pieces were manoeuvred in such a way to aim at your vehicles, the question may occur to some in the courtroom as if these are fairly large guns, how that might be possible. Can you assist the Chamber, perhaps, in understanding and in terms of the location of these guns in relation to where your vehicles were located, how much had to be done to put these guns on a track where they were aiming at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Since the -- they did not have to move much target us. There was no need to remove the weapons from the -- from their emplacements. It was simply with a slight manoeuvre that this truck could be lowered -- that the gun could be lowered, and to direct it a little to the left or to the right to aim at our position. That is what I think what they did. And they did not have to really lift to move truly the guns. To move them from the positions where there were, a slight manoeuvre was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, apart from those two artillery pieces that you've just told us about, as you moved about that day, did you see any other larger weapons -- perhaps not of the calibre, but other types of weapons other than -- I guess what I'm saying -- other than hand-held infantry weapons that were firing on Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: As for artillery pieces, these were the only ones that I saw. One could hear other artillery pieces whilst we were on the hill observing Mostar, but I do not know what was the origin of that. I know that they were machine guns, 60, and that they were targeting the headquarters of the 41st Brigade of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you see anti-aircraft guns being used in a direct-fire role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Indeed. The anti-aircraft weapons were being used in the attack on the headquarters of the 41st Brigade of the BH army. They were being used against terrestrial targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And perhaps it would assist -- I shouldn't assume too much. When I asked you a moment ago "in a direct-fire role," what is direct fire -- from an artillery perspective, what is direct fire in contrast to other types of fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: In artillery, this is the -- there is direct support and indirect support. The direct support is the fire used to support the attack of one's unit. Indirect artillery support is used to support another different unit, that is, to reinforce the artillery fire of the other unit. In this case, when I speak about anti-aircraft weapons, I'm talking about the direct fire from these firearms, that is, direct fire, direct, not in a curve, but to achieve another sector. And its target could be -- that is, when I say that, I mean a target that could be seen directly from the place -- from the place of the origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure how much to stay on this, but perhaps it may be of some significance. Can you explain to the Chamber the difference between the type of fire that's artillery fire that is fired by something called a howitzer as opposed to the artillery fire by something called a gun? Is one used in a direct-fire mode and the other one primarily firing in a more trajectory or arc?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, in an arc, which means an indirect sector, it is usually done by mortars and, that is, it is used to fire at targets behind a hill, behind an elevation and to go over an obstacle. And an artillery shot allows this type of fire, and it is quite precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The two anti-aircraft guns that you saw that day, just to finish on this, were they firing in this direct-fire way, in terms of a direct line of sight, to the ABiH headquarters in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: The artillery, that is, the gunfire, the fire from the gun they were firing at Mostar, I do not know where the projectiles fell because I could not see that. I could only see the guns firing of -- 50 millimetres of the anti-aircraft weapons, and they were firing precisely at the headquarters of the 41st Brigade of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you assist the Chamber, please, in the approximation of these anti-aircraft guns in terms of, for instance, one of the roads coming into Mostar or some other feature that may assist you in giving the Judges some idea of the location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: They were on both sides of the road connecting Mostar with Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Later that day, approximately at 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon, did you arrive back at Medjugorje to your base and report to Colonel Morales or Major Acuna, as the case might be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, I informed both commanders, Colonel Morales and Major Acuna. And it was decided to issue a public communication about these incidents. And I do not know if this was the same tape or a copy of the tape that we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had -- we sent to a journalist in Split, a journalist whose name was Angeles Rodicio. We wanted to show that an attack had begun from the west part of Mostar against the east side, that HVO was attacking the BH army, and make it abundantly clear -- and make abundantly clear the information that Radio Mostar was saying and what our interpreters said was the information about the beginning of an attack, that Radio Mostar was saying that the BH army had launched an attack on the HVO. This tape --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Let me stop you there for a moment, please. Based on what you personally saw on the 9th of May, can you tell this Chamber whether these broadcasts by Radio Mostar saying that the ABiH had started the attack were those broadcast -- were those statements false?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, from what we could see. And from what we had -- were being told from the beginning, our patrols, or rather, a patrol - because there was only one patrol which we had on the hill - the attack was being launched by the HVO against the east side of Mostar, that is, the Muslim part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you started to say something, I think, and I interrupted you - I apologise - about this tape being given to a Spanish journalist. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, this journalist received the tape, and on the news the same evening over Spanish television, images were shown and the commentary said that an attack had taken place in Mostar, the HVO against the Muslims in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After -- well, after that, after the broadcast of this videotape, were the Spanish Battalion's movements restricted, further restricted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Logically speaking, there was discomfort in the highest spheres of HVO, because they knew that it was only us who would be able to have recorded this tape, and for this reason, we were no longer allowed to enter Mostar. And the unit that was inside, that before had been displaced from the area because of the attack, remained isolated and could no longer receive support from us up to a day later, if I remember correctly. But from that time on, we were checked in all our movements, and they tried to find out whether we had video cameras or cameras taking films. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, I'm about to go to a different topic, but perhaps having a military man here, we should take advantage of that in one additional respect. I asked you some questions a few minutes go about anti-aircraft guns. In your military education and experience, have you ever heard of a gun that may be commonly referred to as a Bofors and if that's considered in some roles to be anti-aircraft weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. Bofors are double-barrel or three-barrel guns that are used against aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether one of the guns that you saw on the road going to Siroki Brijeg on the 9th of May was one of those Bofors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After the events of the 9th and 10th of May, did you continue to stay in touch with Ivan Andabak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I kept in touch not only with Colonel Andabak but with all the military sources, people I knew from the HVO and from the BH army, and this with the objective of continuing to find out about the plans of both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During these continuing conversations, did Mr. Andabak say anything more to you about not only his personal objectives but what the objectives of the HVO were during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that his objective was to try and get all the Muslims out and that this was being very difficult to do because he had not expected such resistance, and he thought it would have been easier to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, after the dinner at Andabak's house that you told us about this morning, did you ever see this man Tuta again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It's nothing that we had scheduled at all. It was a casual encounter. In Siroki Brijeg, we met in the street, very quickly had a conversation. I saw that he had a military uniform on. I don't know whether his rank was on the sleeve; I didn't really notice. And we had a brief conversation. I realised he seemed to be quite satisfied that the war had begun and that he expected the war to come to a successful end, namely, getting the Muslims displaced from the city of Mostar. And all this were just sentences in our conversation, but of course it was a conversation carried out with movements of the hand, with -- in Italian; this is how I was able to understand what Mr. Tuta was saying to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness LL, you've previously expressed the view that it was difficult sometimes to figure out exactly where this Tuta fit in the organisation of things; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I believe that question assumes facts not in evidence. I've not heard this witness testify to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Mr. President. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, as you were conducting this information-gathering role, can you tell the Chamber whether or not you -- whether it was easy or you had some difficulty in trying to assess exactly where this Tuta fit in the picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, I'm a military man; therefore, it's rather easy for me to get in contact with persons who belong to an army, to people who are in contact with troops and people who are fighting alongside the troops. This was the case of Ivan Andabak. And Mr. Andabak had told me this and other military men from HVO and other military men from the army. However, in the case of Mr. Tuta [Realtime transcript omitted "Tuta"] he himself is the one that told me when we had dinner together in the house of Colonel Andabak that under his orders, he had several brigadiers and several colonels. However, I did know that he was not a military man. But we all know that in a civil war situation, a person that brings money to the cause, that fights for this cause, who forgets about his earlier life in order to dedicate himself completely to the cause, the cause that he considers to be a just cause, it's only normal that he be given a place in the military institution. And this is what I understood. This is what I saw. This is what was expressed by Mr. Tuta. However, even though I did realise that the chiefs of the brigades that we had received information about were other people, but I believe that he was dealing with planning, with controlling operations, leading operations in a sporadic fashion, leading combat activities, and this was confirmed to me by several military sources of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me clarify a couple of things, Witness LL. Again, for the purposes of the transcript, you said, "However, in the case of Mr. ..." and then there's a blank in the transcript, "... he himself is the one that told me when we had dinner together ..." So who is the person that you're referring to there, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Yes. It was Mr. Tuta who told me when we were speaking at this dinner party that he, under his command, under his orders, he had several colonels and brigadiers of the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you about the conclusions that you reached about this Mr. Tuta. Can you tell the Chamber how many times during your tour of duty in 1993 did you see this Mr. Tuta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS LL
utterances.text: Well, exactly how many times, I cannot say. But two organised meetings, at least one when we had dinner with Colonel Ivan Andabak, and another meeting in Mostar -- no, I'm sorry, in Medjugorje, with Colonel Zorzo in the meeting. And then later on, in a sporadic fashion, one more meeting that I already mentioned, and perhaps another meeting more.
